newsitem.title: CANADA: Ontario nuclear shutdown sparks enviromental fears.
newsitem.headline: Ontario nuclear shutdown sparks enviromental fears.

text.p: The nuclear woes of Ontario Hydro, North America's biggest power utility, have sparked environmental fears and questions about the future of atomic energy in Canada.

The utility's planned switch to fossil fuels during a massive overhaul of its troubled nuclear power plants will boost output of pollutants that cause acid rain and global warming, environmentalists say.

Ontario government-owned Ontario Hydro unveiled plans on Wednesday to suspend seven Candu nuclear units and revamp its remaining 12-unit operation. The overhaul is expected to cost up to C$8 billion ($5.7 billion) over the next five years.

Industry critics said the shakeup was a mortal blow to nuclear power in Canada and might hasten the demise of Ontario Hydro's 91-year-old power monopoly in Canada's richest and most populous province.
"The nuclear option is dead," Tom Adams, executive director of Energy Probe, said in a telephone interview on Friday.

"The remaining reactors in service in Canada will continue to operate for a few more years and wind down to ultimately a non-nuclear Canada," said Adams, whose group has monitored Ontario's nuclear industry for 30 years.
Aside from concern over disposing of nuclear waste and radioactive containment leaks, environmental groups said the cost had been too high.
The utility is struggling under C$33 billion ($24 billion) of debt, due partly to costly nuclear plant construction.

There are 22 Candu nuclear reactors in operation in Ontario, Quebec and New Brunswick. The oldest reactors -- brought into service in the early 1970s in Ontario -- are among those scheduled to close later this year.
Ontario Energy Minister Norm Sterling defended nuclear power, saying it "has a great advantage in terms of emissions and it's unfortunate we can't continue to produce power in that way."

Ontario Hydro is the continent's largest electricity producer based on installed generating capacity. It operates 69 hydro-electric stations, five nuclear stations and six fossil-fuel plants in Canada's industrial heartland.

The overhaul followed a scathing report on Wednesday that said the nuclear division suffered from a "lack of authoritative and accountable managerial leadership" and concluded the plants' performance was "minimally acceptable."
But it said the Candu reactor, designed and built by federally-owned Atomic Energy of Canada Ltd. and also used in Argentina, Romania and South Korea, was a "robust" design.
Environmentalists welcomed the nuclear shutdown, but they slammed the decision to boost output from coal and oil-fired plants to replace the lost power.
Greenpeace estimated the move would increase emissions from fossil fuel plants by between 300 and 400 percent.
"As a result of this decision we can also expect increased acid rain, more damage to human health, and even early death because of increased levels of smog," Greenpeace said.

Ontario Hydro said the use of coal with low sulphur content would enable it to keep emission levels below provincial acid-gas emission targets despite a 60 percent increase in electricity produced by fossil fuels.
"We will...fully comply with acid gas emission regulations," said Ontario Hydro chairman Bill Farlinger.
